altText: A small still life of poppies and daisies, painted in strong reds, yellows, whites and blacks against a dark background.

context: A small oil painting on cardboard made around 1867 by the French artist Odilon Redon. The Art Institute's record lists poppies and daisies, with red, black, white and yellow, as subjects, and its exhibition history shows the work was once shown under the French title Coquelicots & Marguerites. The record gives no further description.

descriptions.k: Look at the flowers! There are red poppies and white daisies. A little yellow shines too. The paint is thick and bright. The picture is small. Can you find a poppy? Can you find a daisy?
descriptions.g12: Odilon Redon painted a small bouquet of poppies and daisies. The poppies are bright red and the daisies are white with yellow centers. The background is dark so the flowers glow. Which flower do you see first? How does the paint make them look soft?
descriptions.g35: Odilon Redon painted this small bouquet around 1867 on cardboard, a surface that is only about 7 by 9 inches. The museum lists poppies, daisies, and the colors red, black, white, and yellow. Redon later became famous for dreamy, mysterious art. Look at how the bright flowers glow. Why might a dark background make colors seem stronger?
descriptions.g68: Redon painted this still life of poppies and daisies around 1867, on a small piece of cardboard about 7 by 9 inches. The Art Institute lists red, black, white, and yellow among its subjects and notes that it was once exhibited as Coquelicots & Marguerites. Redon would later be known for imaginative, dreamlike works. How do bold color and loose handling make simple flowers feel alive? What does a small format change about how you look?
descriptions.g910: This small oil on cardboard (c. 1867) shows poppies and daisies in strong red, yellow, white, and black. Though Redon later became known for visionary, dreamlike imagery, here he studies flowers with direct color and paint. The museum record offers no description, only subjects and exhibition history, including the French title Coquelicots & Marguerites. How does contrast between vivid blossoms and dark ground create impact, and what can a modest study reveal about an artist's range?
descriptions.g1112: Redon's c. 1867 flower study on cardboard predates the symbolist imagery for which he is best known. The Art Institute lists poppies, daisies, and red, black, white and yellow, and records exhibitions under the title Coquelicots & Marguerites. The record offers no interpretation. Does this intimate, small-scale still life anticipate Redon's later preoccupation with color and mystery, or should it be understood on its own terms? What visual evidence supports each reading?

teacherNote.context: A small oil on cardboard from around 1867 by Odilon Redon. The Art Institute lists poppies, daisies, and the colors red, black, white and yellow, and records exhibitions under the title Coquelicots & Marguerites. The record has no description.
directions: Have students paint a small bouquet on dark paper and compare how colors glow against it versus against white.
Ask students to give the painting a title in another language they know or look up, and discuss what stays the same.
Discuss how a small painting can feel as important as a large one.
